topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European public health context; findings may have limited applicability to Australian healthcare settings, which operate under different regulatory frameworks, funding models, and digital infrastructure priorities.
takeaways: Map your organisation's current digital competency gaps against a structured European framework to identify priority upskilling areas in AI and digital tools relevant to health service delivery.

Use this scoping review to benchmark competency expectations across different professional roles (clinical, administrative, technical) in your sector, then adapt the framework to Australian regulatory and workplace contexts.
Consider which 'digital public health' competencies (data literacy, digital communication, technology adoption) overlap with general AI literacy needs in your workforce.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focused on faculty development in public health education contexts. Findings may not generalise to non-academic settings or other disciplinary fields. Geographic scope unclear from title.
takeaways: Design faculty development programs that address psychological barriers to AI adoption, not just technical skills — focus on shifting mindsets from resistance to readiness before introducing tools.
Position educators themselves as early adopters and champions of AI literacy; their confidence and enthusiasm directly shapes student readiness and organisational culture around AI.

Embed AI literacy into existing curricula through faculty coaching and peer-learning communities rather than standalone workshops — this addresses contextual concerns specific to public health practice.

articles.title: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies - Sage Journals
articles.snippet: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies  Sage Journals
articles.generalisability: Limited specificity — the snippet provides no detail on geographic scope, sample size, or methodological approach. Likely focuses on general educational strategies rather than location-specific findings.
takeaways: Identify which specific AI competencies (e.g., prompt engineering, data literacy, AI ethics) are most critical for your workforce and design targeted upskilling programs around those gaps rather than generic AI awareness.

Consider how educational strategies can be scaffolded for different employee cohorts — Generation Z may have different learning preferences and baseline familiarity than older staff, requiring tailored delivery methods and content depth.

Evaluate whether your current training approach addresses both technical skills and broader AI literacy (understanding limitations, bias, responsible use) — both are essential for effective workforce preparation.

articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature

takeaways: AI competencies should be embedded within a broader digital literacy framework rather than taught in isolation, integrating technical skills, critical thinking, and ethical understanding.
Holistic approaches to AI education at foundational levels (middle school) may inform how organisations structure AI upskilling programmes for employees with varying baseline digital competencies.

articles.title: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — proposes a theoretical framework for higher education contexts, but generalisability to other sectors and non-academic organisations unclear without seeing full methodology and validation data.
takeaways: AI literacy functions as a meta-skill (enabling mastery of other skills) rather than a standalone technical competency — design your AI capability programmes to build foundational understanding that transfers across roles and tools.

A four-domain model may structure AI literacy development more effectively than single-track approaches — consider how your organisation's AI training addresses multiple interconnected dimensions rather than isolated technical skills.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on higher education context, which may not directly transfer to organisational or workplace settings. Geographic scope unclear from snippet.
takeaways: Identify which AI competencies are most relevant to your workforce (technical skills, literacy, ethical reasoning) and prioritise upskilling in those areas rather than attempting broad coverage.
Consider whether structured training programs, integration into existing curricula, or peer-learning approaches work best for your organisation's context and employee cohorts.
Assess baseline AI literacy levels before implementation to tailor content difficulty and delivery method to actual employee needs.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — without access to full methodology details from the snippet alone, generalisability depends on sample size, sector diversity, and geographic scope, which cannot be determined.
takeaways: Understanding approach-avoidance dynamics helps explain why some employees proactively reshape their roles around AI while others resist or withdraw — use this insight to identify which team members need support versus those ready to lead AI integration.

Job crafting behaviours reveal individual differences in AI adoption: design targeted interventions that either encourage approach-oriented crafting (expanding AI-complementary tasks) or address avoidance patterns (alleviating AI-displacement anxiety) depending on employee response type.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited to organisations operating under paternalistic leadership models; findings may not generalise to flat or distributed leadership structures common in Western tech companies. Geographic scope not specified from title.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools by involving employees in customising or 'crafting' how AI is configured and used in their workflows — this strengthens collaboration rather than resistance.

In paternalistic leadership contexts, position AI adoption as a leader-endorsed initiative that respects employee autonomy in implementation, leveraging the trust inherent in this leadership style to drive adoption.

Design AI implementation programmes that explicitly create opportunities for employees to shape AI use cases relevant to their work, as this ownership mindset mediates the relationship between leadership support and actual AI adoption.

articles.title: AI usage and employee creativity: the mediating role of work engagement and the moderating role of technology acceptance - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI usage and employee creativity: the mediating role of work engagement and the moderating role of technology acceptance  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The model tested (AI usage → work engagement → creativity, moderated by technology acceptance) is theoretically sound but applicability may vary by organisational context, industry sector, and employee demographics.
takeaways: Work engagement appears to be a key mechanism through which AI tools influence employee creativity — invest in understanding and supporting engagement levels when rolling out AI capabilities, not just tool adoption.

Technology acceptance (employee attitudes toward AI) moderates the relationship, suggesting adoption initiatives must address psychological barriers and perceptions of usefulness, not just provide access to tools.

When implementing AI to enhance creativity, focus on both the tool itself and the human factors (engagement and acceptance) that determine whether employees will actually use AI in ways that unlock creative potential.

articles.title: Psychological safety mediates link between AI adoption and worker depression - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Psychological safety mediates link between AI adoption and worker depression  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from title and snippet alone — would depend on study design, sample size, and whether findings are from a specific sector or geography. The relationship between AI adoption, psychological safety, and mental health outcomes requires careful contextual consideration.
takeaways: Psychological safety is a critical protective factor when introducing AI tools — organisations that foster open communication and trust during AI implementation may reduce negative mental health impacts on workers.

Before rolling out AI systems, assess and strengthen psychological safety in teams; workers who fear negative consequences or feel unsafe speaking up about AI concerns are at higher risk of depression and disengagement.

Create explicit channels for workers to voice concerns about AI adoption without career consequences, and ensure leadership actively addresses fears about job security or capability gaps rather than dismissing them.

articles.title: “Under the Shadow of Uncertainty”: the mediating role of job stress and the AI self-efficacy as a shield in cybersecurity behavior | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: “Under the Shadow of Uncertainty”: the mediating role of job stress and the AI self-efficacy as a shield in cybersecurity behavior | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not provided in snippet. The focus on cybersecurity professionals suggests sector-specific findings that may not transfer directly to other employee populations, though the psychological mechanisms (job stress, self-efficacy) are broadly relevant.
takeaways: Building AI self-efficacy in cybersecurity teams can buffer against job stress and support better security behaviours — consider targeted training and confidence-building in AI tools relevant to your security workflows.
Job stress appears to undermine cybersecurity compliance; addressing workload and pressure alongside AI capability development may yield better outcomes than focusing on either factor alone.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full methodology — depends on sample characteristics, sector focus, and geographic scope. Psychological capital theory has broad applicability, but findings about AI as a job resource may be limited by the specific work contexts studied.
takeaways: Build psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) in teams working with AI systems — employees with higher psychological capital are better positioned to view AI as a tool that enhances rather than threatens their work.

Frame AI integration as a job resource opportunity during change communication — this reframing can unlock innovation and engagement rather than triggering defensive responses or compliance-only adoption.

Assess and develop psychological capital through targeted interventions (goal-setting, skills development, peer support, optimism-building) alongside AI upskilling — the two are mutually reinforcing for innovation outcomes.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without specified empirical data or geographic scope. Insights may reflect US business school viewpoint and may not generalise to Australian organisational contexts or non-US labour markets.
takeaways: Identify specific work processes in your organisation where AI is already reshaping roles, then engage employees in conversations about how their work is changing rather than waiting for disruption to occur unmanaged.
Use AI adoption as a trigger for behaviour change by framing upskilling as an immediate professional development need, not a future concern — this creates urgency that motivates behavioural shifts.
Map out which job categories in your organisation face the most significant AI-driven role changes, then prioritise change communication and support interventions for those groups first.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from title and snippet alone — full article needed to assess sample characteristics, geographic scope, sector coverage, and methodological rigor.
takeaways: AI adoption can trigger either approach (seeking new opportunities) or avoidance (withdrawing or resisting) responses in employees — understanding which motivational direction dominates in your team helps tailor change management and upskilling support.

Job crafting (how employees actively shape their roles) may be a key lever: employees who feel empowered to reshape their work around AI are more likely to engage constructively rather than resist, so consider creating explicit space for employees to experiment with and reshape their roles as tools change.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG analysis likely draws on their consulting client base (predominantly large enterprises across multiple sectors and geographies), but specific sample composition and methodology not detailed in snippet. Findings most applicable to large organisations with resources for systematic transformation programmes.
takeaways: Position AI capability development as a workforce transformation initiative, not just a technology rollout — this framing helps align HR, leadership, and employees around shared change objectives rather than treating it as an IT-only project.

Design reskilling and upskilling programmes that account for workforce demographics and role-specific AI needs — one-size-fits-all training is less effective than targeted capability building linked to actual job requirements and career pathways.

Establish clear accountability structures and change management processes to embed AI literacy across teams — without organisational commitment to supporting employees through the transition, even well-resourced AI initiatives face adoption and retention risks.

articles.title: Advancing applied behavioral science: the GAP framework - Nature
articles.snippet: Advancing applied behavioral science: the GAP framework  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents a theoretical framework (GAP) for applied behavioral science that is likely globally applicable, but specific implementation examples and evidence base are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: The GAP framework (likely Goal, Action, Prompt or similar) offers a structured approach to designing behavioural interventions; familiarise yourself with its components to systematically diagnose where behaviour change initiatives typically fail.

Use the framework to audit your current behaviour change efforts — identify whether gaps exist in goal clarity, action design, or implementation prompts, then target interventions at the weakest link rather than broad programmatic changes.

articles.title: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting experience across industries, but specific case examples and client contexts not detailed in snippet. Findings likely most applicable to large organisations with resources for structured change programmes.
takeaways: Frame AI upskilling as a strategic organisational change initiative, not just a training programme — this shifts buy-in from HR alone to senior leadership and helps secure sustained investment and governance.

Design change management infrastructure alongside skill-building (e.g., clear communication, stakeholder mapping, resistance management) to increase adoption and reduce the gap between training completion and actual AI capability use.

Align upskilling with business imperatives and role-specific workflows rather than generic AI literacy — employees are more likely to engage when they see direct application to their daily work and career progression.

articles.title: Inclusive algorithmic work design: the moderating role of DEI interventions and diversity-supportive culture in AI-driven workplace transformation - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Inclusive algorithmic work design: the moderating role of DEI interventions and diversity-supportive culture in AI-driven workplace transformation  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study design and sample characteristics, which are not evident from the title and snippet alone. The focus on DEI interventions and diversity-supportive culture suggests potential applicability across sectors, but specific limitations regarding geography, organisation size, and industry context cannot be assessed without accessing the full paper.
takeaways: When implementing AI-driven workplace changes, actively design algorithms and processes with inclusivity as a core principle rather than treating it as an afterthought — this is more effective than remedial interventions alone.

Establish or strengthen diversity-supportive cultural norms in your organisation before or during AI transformation, as culture acts as a buffer that moderates whether DEI interventions actually stick and create lasting behaviour change.

Combine both structural DEI interventions (policies, training, hiring practices) with cultural change efforts (leadership modelling, inclusive communication, psychological safety) — neither works optimally in isolation during algorithmic work design.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline framing suggests sensationalism typical of science news reporting; actual study details not provided in snippet, making it impossible to assess methodological rigor or sample representativeness.
takeaways: Brain imaging studies often produce striking visuals and headlines, but the gap between 'difference detected' and 'clinically meaningful or predictive' is often wider than media coverage suggests.

The term 'psychopath' encompasses a spectrum of traits; brain scan findings may reflect specific sub-populations rather than a clear categorical distinction, which is why the framing as 'shocking' warrants healthy skepticism.

Neurobiological differences are fascinating, but they don't determine behaviour or destiny — this kind of research is interesting precisely because it challenges simple nature-vs-nurture thinking about personality and conduct.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — sample size, geographic scope, and methodology not provided. Generalisability depends on whether wine reviews analyzed were from diverse sources and whether personality patterns hold across different wine-drinking populations.
takeaways: What people write about wine reveals personality traits in unexpected ways — linguistic choices in reviews can signal broader personality patterns, suggesting our everyday preferences leak clues about who we are.
AI can spot personality signals in seemingly mundane text that humans might miss, opening new ways to understand personality beyond traditional self-report questionnaires.
Wine preferences and the language used to describe them aren't just about taste — they're a window into how different personality types perceive and communicate about their experiences.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Twin studies typically use Western samples (often UK or Scandinavia); findings may reflect cultural and institutional contexts specific to those regions and may not generalise equally across all political systems or cultures.
takeaways: Twin studies reveal that authoritarian political beliefs have a measurable genetic component — suggesting it's not purely learned ideology but shaped partly by inherited traits like preference for order and hierarchy.

The findings are counterintuitive because political beliefs feel like conscious choices, yet heritable personality factors appear to nudge people toward or away from authoritarian worldviews — a reminder that politics isn't just rational reasoning.

This research highlights why people with genuinely different underlying temperaments can honestly disagree on governance and social structure — it's not just misinformation or stupidity, but different psychological starting points.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample size and composition, which are not detailed in the snippet. The findings likely apply to general adult populations but scope is unclear without access to full methodology.
takeaways: People remember surprising events differently depending on their personality — your natural traits influence how your brain encodes unexpected moments, not just what happens.

This suggests personality isn't just about how you behave socially; it shapes fundamental cognitive processes like memory encoding, which is a counterintuitive link between stable traits and basic brain function.

The finding reveals why eyewitness accounts of the same surprising event can vary wildly — it's not just attention or stress, but personality-driven differences in how memories are stored in the first place.

articles.title: New relationships take a surprising physical toll on older adults - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New relationships take a surprising physical toll on older adults  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — based on a single study with unclear sample size and demographic details; findings may not generalise across different cultural contexts or relationship types.
takeaways: Entering a new relationship in later life comes with measurable physical costs — a counterintuitive finding that challenges the assumption that companionship is universally health-promoting.
The stress of forming new bonds and adjusting to partnership dynamics in older age appears to outweigh the typical health benefits of relationships, at least initially.
This quirky finding reminds us that life stage matters enormously — what benefits a 30-year-old may stress a 70-year-old, even when the basic experience (new relationship) is the same.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: High — findings suggest universal links between personality and music taste across diverse global populations, though specific cultural variations in music genres may apply differently by region.
takeaways: Your taste in music genuinely reveals something about your personality — it's not just social posturing. The connection between what you listen to and who you are appears consistent across cultures worldwide.

What's surprising: musical preferences seem to transcend cultural boundaries in predicting personality traits, suggesting that personality might shape musical taste through universal human psychology rather than purely through cultural socialisation.

A fun dinner party fact: if you know someone's music preferences, you can make surprisingly accurate guesses about their broader personality traits — whether they're open to new experiences, conscientious, or extroverted — regardless of where they're from.

articles.snippet: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams  Frontiers

takeaways: AI tools can potentially support inclusive leadership practices that reduce gendered disparities in multicultural teams — consider how your organisation might pilot AI-assisted mechanisms to flag unconscious bias in team dynamics and decision-making.

The interaction between AI systems and human leadership behaviour matters; simply implementing AI tools without deliberate inclusive leadership practices may not improve psychological safety or gendered outcomes in diverse teams.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad global reach, but representativeness depends on PwC's sampling methodology and respondent demographics, which are not detailed in the snippet. Results may skew toward PwC's typical client base (large organisations, developed economies).
takeaways: Use survey data to benchmark your organisation's psychological safety climate against global and industry peers—identify specific fears (e.g., job security, AI impact) your workforce shares and address them through targeted communication and policy changes.

Map 'hopes' themes from the survey to concrete development opportunities—if employees hope for upskilling or clearer career progression, link this to your AI capability-building initiatives to build buy-in and psychological safety around technological change.

Monitor shifts in workforce sentiment year-on-year using this survey as a reference point; if your organisation's safety and engagement metrics diverge from global trends, investigate root causes in your leadership, systems, or change management approach.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The conceptual model (AI adoption → psychological safety → depression) may apply across sectors, but geographic scope, industry focus, and sample size would determine applicability to Australian organisational contexts.
takeaways: AI adoption can erode psychological safety if not paired with transparent, ethical leadership — leaders should explicitly communicate ethical decision-making in AI implementation to protect employee wellbeing.
Monitor psychological safety as a key outcome when rolling out AI tools; declining safety may signal depression risk, warranting intervention through team dialogue and clarified ethical guidelines.
Ethical leadership is a protective factor against depression during AI transitions — invest in leader capability to model and discuss ethical AI use, not just technical rollout.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Limited — BCG report likely draws on consulting experience and client examples, but lacks detail on sample composition, geographic scope, and research methodology. Findings may reflect primarily large, multinational organisations that engage consulting firms.
takeaways: Create explicit norms that invite input from all levels and backgrounds; psychological safety reduces the 'voice penalty' experienced by employees from underrepresented groups, enabling broader talent contribution and decision-making quality.

Leaders should model vulnerability and respond non-defensively to questions or dissent; this signals that risk-taking is safe and is foundational to levelling dynamics where junior, female, and minority employees feel equally empowered to speak up.

Assess and monitor psychological safety regularly through confidential surveys or listening sessions; organisations that measure it can identify pockets where certain teams or demographics feel unsafe and intervene with targeted leadership coaching or team norms work.

articles.title: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024 - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: US-focused findings on workplace psychological safety; may have limited applicability to Australian workplace contexts due to differences in employment law, workplace culture, and organisational practices. Findings reflect American workforce demographics and workplace trends.
takeaways: Identify specific barriers to psychological safety in your team (e.g., fear of speaking up, lack of manager receptiveness) using APA's framework, then prioritise interventions targeting the highest-impact barriers first.
Use the report's data on psychological safety trends to benchmark your organisation's current state and set measurable goals for improvement over 12–24 months.
Train managers on the link between psychological safety and employee wellbeing outcomes (engagement, retention, performance) to build business case for cultural change initiatives in your workplace.

articles.title: Why Employees Aren’t Transparent About Their AI Usage - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Why Employees Aren’t Transparent About Their AI Usage  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Moderate — likely reflects practices in US and similar Western knowledge economies, but lacks empirical grounding. Applicability to Australian workplaces depends on local organisational cultures and regulatory context around AI use disclosure.
takeaways: Employees hide AI tool usage due to fear of job security concerns, performance judgement, or policy violation — create explicit psychological safety by clarifying what AI use is encouraged, permitted, or prohibited, and detach usage from performance metrics.

Transparency barriers stem from ambiguity about organisational AI policies — establish clear, written guidelines on approved tools and use cases, then actively communicate them and model open AI adoption from leadership to reduce perceptions of risk.

Build trust through non-punitive feedback channels where employees can ask questions about AI tool appropriateness without career risk — this removes the pressure to hide usage and enables better governance of actual risks.
